title: SPACE CHASE – Complete Game Specification (+6 more)

lines.s: Balance game from body sway: `src/games/wobbleisland/` (`sway.ts` pure maths, `constants.ts`, `engine.ts`, `index.tsx`). The first game that reads **acceleration**.

- **Registry flags:** `requiresStrengthTest: false` (no Pre-Game grip test gates it, `useGameSession` skips `test_required`, and the Take Test button is hidden), `requiresCalibration: false` (no Table/Wall picker, no Set Zero) and `streams: { acceleration: true }` only. `GameHost` subscribes `facade.acceleration$` just for games that declare it and writes `GameProps.accelerationRef(x, y, z)` in the active phases. Every game declares `streams` (see "Stream contract per game" in `docs/spec/sensor-architecture.md`).

- **Sway measure:** the engine's first 3 s of play are a still baseline (the mean reading, gravity included, so any resting orientation works); after that sway is the rolling 1 s RMS of the vector difference from the baseline, in g. Backends already emit g (Android/iOS/web: Sensor Fusion bias-corrected acceleration; Playwork BLE: raw accelerometer g; mock: tilt in g), so the adapter only needs the baseline subtraction. **Unverified on a real PLAYBALL** (stream rate and suitability are checked after the build, A2); rotation is not used as a second signal yet (A7).

- **Game:** the island rises while sway is under the limit and sinks gradually (faster the further over) otherwise; score is 10 points per second times the level times island height. Every 30 s the level rises and the limit tightens 10% (floor 40%). The sway limit is `GameConfig.swayLimitG` (trainer slider, 0.02-0.30 g) and each preset sets it (Easy 0.15, Medium 0.12, Hard 0.08, Sprint 0.05). Eyes open only, visual feedback only, no sound cue and no safety notice (A1/A4/A9/A11).

- **Body part and side:** the standard funnel selection is used and saved on the session as usual; there is no exercise-position setting, the physiotherapist defines the position outside the app (A8/A12).

- **Result:** `GameResult.stabilityRmsG` is the RMS sway over the whole session after the baseline (lower is steadier). The Progress Report has a **Balance** section (best-of-day, lower is better) with a note to compare only sessions in the same exercise position (A10).
- Music is a placeholder copy of the Asteroid loop. Manual article `wobble-island` (English only).
**Space Chase** is a 2D side-scrolling space arcade game designed for stabilized isometric strength training using the Smart PLAYBALL.
The player controls a spaceship traveling from left to right through space.
The game trains two independent physical abilities simultaneously:
1. **Isometric Strength:** The player must generate and maintain a minimum target force using PLAYBALL.
2. **Isometric Stability:** The player must maintain PLAYBALL stability to keep the spaceship aligned with its intended flight path.
The game must clearly distinguish between these two abilities:
- Ball stability controls vertical spaceship movement and deviation from the intended flight path.
The player is chased by an enemy spaceship from behind and must navigate through asteroid fields.
The game is designed for rehabilitation patients and must be enjoyable, accessible, calm, and visually engaging without excessive stimulation.
The game supports different exercise types and body parts, including:
- Static squat exercises using a large PLAYBALL.
- Other suitable isometric exercises using Smart PLAYBALL.
The game must use only the following two sensor measurements:
Force controls the spaceship's horizontal speed.
- When force is equal to or above the current Target Force, the spaceship's engine operates effectively and the ship moves forward faster.
- Higher force may provide a greater speed advantage.
- When force falls below the Target Force, the engine weakens and the enemy spaceship gradually gets closer.
- Force must never control vertical movement or flight direction.
Target Force is a minimum threshold, not a force value that the patient must match exactly.
Any force equal to or above the Target Force satisfies the force requirement.
There is no upper force limit for achievement.
### 2.2 Accelerometer – Ball Stability and Vertical Movement
The accelerometer measures movement and acceleration fluctuations of PLAYBALL.
These measurements are used to estimate ball stability.
- Stable PLAYBALL: the spaceship remains aligned with its intended flight path.
- Unstable PLAYBALL: the spaceship deviates vertically from the intended flight path.
- Greater instability produces greater vertical deviation.
- When stability improves, the spaceship gradually returns toward the intended flight path.
Accelerometer data must not control horizontal speed.
Stability must not affect the score directly.

The actual accelerometer signal processing, calibration, filtering, stability classification, and mapping to spaceship movement must be determined by reviewing the real PLAYBALL sensor characteristics and available sensor data.
Do not invent arbitrary acceleration thresholds without validating them against actual PLAYBALL behavior.
The separation between the two controls is essential:
| Ball Stability | Vertical deviation from intended path | Horizontal speed |
The game must preserve this separation throughout all gameplay modes and difficulty presets.
- The spaceship travels from left to right.
- The player's spaceship remains generally at a stable horizontal position on the screen.
- An enemy spaceship follows the player from behind, on the left.
- Asteroids appear ahead of the player throughout all stages.
- The player must maintain sufficient force to escape the enemy and sufficient stability to navigate safely through the asteroid field.
The game must not feel like a shooter.
There are no weapons, shooting mechanics, lasers, missiles, or projectiles.
The player controls a friendly, modern-looking spaceship.
- Optional subtle visual feedback when the spaceship deviates from its intended path.
The spaceship should be visually distinguishable from the enemy.
The enemy spaceship follows the player from behind.
Its behavior is controlled exclusively by the player's Force performance.
- When Force is at or above Target Force, the player gains distance from the enemy.
- When Force falls below Target Force, the enemy gradually approaches.
- The enemy must communicate the physical consequence of insufficient force clearly.
- The enemy does not attack or fire weapons.

changes.title: Data models, auth, identity, sensor identity

lines.s: - **Wiring:** the connect scan enriches each row via `syncIdentity` (name + size badge in `DeviceRow`); registration resolves identity and writes name+size into the license + store (`sensorBallSizeCm` drives force calcs); the boot auto-connect path reconciles in the background (server wins on startup); the global pill shows the cached name + the MAC-tail id.

- **Identity TTL (S-279):** each identify `GET` costs two backend Lambda runs (authorizer + register) against a tiny account concurrency quota, and names/sizes change rarely, so `syncIdentity` returns the local record without a server call when it is in sync (`pendingSync` false) and `updatedAt` is under `IDENTITY_TTL_MS` (6 h). Unparseable or future `updatedAt` counts as stale. A successful empty answer (200 with null name/size, a registered but unnamed ball) is remembered in memory for the same TTL; a 404 or network failure is never cached, because `fetchSensorIdentity` returns `null` for both and offline must retry. Pending edits are always flushed first. The two registration paths (`useSensorConnect`, `secondBallLicense`) pass `{ force: true }` so a newly registered ball adopts the server value. Trade-off: a rename made elsewhere (trainer web UI, another device) shows up here after the TTL or on the next registration, not on the next launch; change `IDENTITY_TTL_MS` to tune it.

- **Ball-size fallback when nothing is known at all (S-296):** unlike name, ball size feeds real downstream math (force conversion), so it must not stay `null` forever. When `syncIdentity` has **no local cache for this MAC at all** and the server answer is also not meaningful (404/offline, or a genuine empty `200`), it returns the smallest supported ball (`BALL_SIZES_CM[0]` = 19cm) as `size` with `name` left `null` — this fallback is never written to `sensorIdentities` (so a later real server answer still overwrites it transparently; the in-memory `emptyAnswerAt` TTL still applies on top). Any local cache, however stale-adjacent, is still preferred over the fallback — the fallback is strictly last-resort. This covers the reported regression where a ball previously named/sized under the old v1 backend (pre S-277/S-281) has no record on the new v2 host and a fresh install has no local cache either, so size silently went missing end-to-end (corner pill, trainer Settings, force display) instead of ever asking the server again or showing a usable number.

- **Ball-size fallback when nothing is known at all (S-296):** unlike name, ball size feeds real downstream math (force conversion), so it must not stay `null` forever. When `syncIdentity` has **no local cache for this MAC at all** and the server answer is also not meaningful (404/offline, or a genuine empty `200`), it returns the smallest supported ball (`BALL_SIZES_CM[0]` = 19cm) as `size` with `name` left `null` — this fallback is never written to `sensorIdentities` or pushed to the server (the About dialog and the panel mark it "assumed"; it is copied into the license record and the store, so every calculation uses 19 cm, never null) (so a later real server answer still overwrites it transparently; the in-memory `emptyAnswerAt` TTL still applies on top). Any local cache, however stale-adjacent, is still preferred over the fallback — the fallback is strictly last-resort. This covers the reported regression where a ball previously named/sized under the old v1 backend (pre S-277/S-281) has no record on the new v2 host and a fresh install has no local cache either, so size silently went missing end-to-end (corner pill, trainer Settings, force display) instead of ever asking the server again or showing a usable number.
## One rule: agents write English, the nightly run translates

- **Agents write only `docs/manual/en/`.** Every skill run that implements something (`finish-ready-stubs`, `spec-work-item`, a sub-agent) updates the English manual and decides the analytics **in the same step**, and records both with `node tools/spec/spec.mjs docs <id> --manual="<slugs | none — reason>" --analytics="<tracked | none — reason>"`. `spec.mjs status <id> in-qa` is refused until both are recorded and every named article exists (backend registry excluded). No agent edits another language folder, `tools/spec-web/documentation/manual-i18n/`, or runs `manual-translate.mjs --save`.

- **Agents write only `docs/manual/en/`.** Every skill run that implements something (`finish-ready-stubs`, `spec-work-item`, a sub-agent) updates the English manual and decides the analytics **in the same step**, and records both with `node tools/spec/spec.mjs docs <id> --manual="<slugs | none — reason>" --analytics="<tracked | none — reason>" --spec="<docs/spec/x.md[#section][, ...] | none — reason>"`. `spec.mjs status <id> in-qa` is refused until all three (spec, manual, analytics) are recorded and every named article exists (backend registry excluded). No agent edits another language folder, `tools/spec-web/documentation/manual-i18n/`, or runs `manual-translate.mjs --save`.

- **The nightly run translates.** `tools/spec/nightly-run.mjs` ends with the manual translation step: `manual-translate.mjs status` (the Ollama container on `OLLAMA_URL`, default `http://localhost:11434`, model `translategemma:12b`; skipped, not failed, when unreachable, and it catches up the next night) then `sync --lang all --save --prune`. It runs after the web build, tests and APK so a long translation never delays them.

- **People may still review.** The spec-web Manual translation tab (Assets) stays for a human to correct a machine translation; a corrected section is not overwritten until its English source changes.
### Two-ball slots (S-267, first piece of S-254)

Full two-ball flow, architecture and open items: `docs/spec/two-ball.md`. Short version: `SensorFacade.forSlot(2)` is a second, independent facade (slot 1 stays the singleton); on native a Playwork ball gets its own `PlayworkBleBackend`, a MetaWear ball is refused with `SecondBallUnsupportedError`.

Full two-ball flow, architecture and open items: `docs/spec/two-ball.md`. Short version: `SensorFacade.forSlot(2)` is a second, independent facade (slot 1 stays the singleton); on native a Playwork ball gets its own `PlayworkBleBackend`, and a MetaWear ball (every real ball) gets its own link in the native plugin (Android: a `Link` per slot, calls carry `slot`; iOS: a second plugin instance, `SensorPlugin2`).

- **Start order (every backend must match):** (1) clear old state: unsubscribe the outputs, `ENABLE` 0, `OUTPUT_ENABLE` [0x00, 0x7F], accel and gyro power off and data disabled, then wait ~150 ms; (2) accelerometer: `CONFIG` [ODR 0x28, 16g range byte for BMI160/BMI270], `DATA_ENABLE` [1, 0], `POWER` 1; (3) gyro: `CONFIG` [0x28, 2000dps], `DATA_ENABLE` [1, 0], `POWER` 1; (4) `MODE` [IMU_PLUS, ranges]; (5) `OUTPUT_ENABLE` [outputMask, **0x00**]; (6) subscribe each wanted output (Euler `0x08`, corrected acc `0x04`); (7) `ENABLE` 1.
- **Stop order:** `ENABLE` 0, `OUTPUT_ENABLE` [0x00, 0x7F], then accel and gyro power off and data disabled.

- **Units:** Euler angles are degrees as sent. Corrected acceleration arrives in **milli-g**; the SDK divides by 1000 (`CorrectedAccelerationData`), so every decoder (`decodeSFCorrectedAcc`, Kotlin, Swift) must too. Forgetting it made every acceleration reading 1000× too large, so Wobble Island sank at once.
- **Output mask bits:** Euler 0x10, corrected acc 0x01 (`sfOutputMask`). `dataEnableMask` in the SDK is per-output; the mask is sent once at start, so changing the wanted set means stop then start.
- **Implemented in:** `SensorPlugin.kt` (Android) and `SensorPlugin.swift` (iOS) follow it; `web-ble.ts` did **not** until S-297 was investigated.

- **No Calibrate button** (S-26 — removed; it previously did nothing meaningful outside a game since no engine exists to hold a `calibrationRef` there. Calibration is only available as part of a game's own flow.)

- **No License Tier row** (S-40 — moved into the About dialog; the panel body was getting crowded and license tier is a lower-frequency lookup than the connection/battery/rotation rows a trainer checks constantly).

- **About** button → dialog showing app version + build, plus **License Tier** (S-26 data, S-40 placement — shown when known: Basic/MyPlayball/Premium, mapped from stored `licenseType` 1/2/3). The About dialog also contains the **Delete User Data** action (see *Delete user data* under Auth & Access).

- **About** button → dialog showing app version + build, plus the **Ball Size** the app is using for its calculations (the store's `sensorBallSizeCm`, the same value as the panel row), marked "(assumed)" when it is the S-296 19 cm last-resort fallback (`useBallSizeAssumed`: fallback size and no saved identity for the MAC, so there is no extra flag to keep in sync; the panel row carries the same marker; string `ball_size_assumed`), plus **License Tier** (S-26 data, S-40 placement — shown when known: Basic/MyPlayball/Premium, mapped from stored `licenseType` 1/2/3). The About dialog also contains the **Delete User Data** action (see *Delete user data* under Auth & Access).

**About version/build — real per-platform identity, not a baked Android number (S-228).** Reported live: iOS's About screen showed "Build 73" when TestFlight actually had "Build 5". Root cause: `VITE_APP_VERSION`/`VITE_APP_BUILD` are injected once at build time from `version.json` (`vite.config.ts`'s `define`) — Android's own `versionName`/`versionCode` — and that's the *one* web bundle both platforms ship, so an iOS build displayed Android's numbering verbatim. iOS's real build identity never comes from `version.json` at all — it comes from App Store Connect directly (`fastlane/Fastfile`'s `beta` lane asks for `latest_testflight_build_number` and uploads `+1`), a completely different, independently-incrementing number. Fixed in `GlobalSensorPill.tsx`: on mount, if `Capacitor.isNativePlatform()`, `@capacitor/app`'s `App.getInfo()` is called — it reads the *actually-installed* bundle's own `CFBundleShortVersionString`/`CFBundleVersion` on iOS or `versionName`/`versionCode` on Android — and overwrites the displayed version/build with the real native values on success. The baked `VITE_APP_VERSION`/`VITE_APP_BUILD` constants stay as the initial value (so About never shows blank while the native call resolves) and as the permanent value on web, where `getInfo()` has no implementation and rejects (caught, logged, ignored — same graceful-no-op pattern as Crashlytics on web). `@capacitor/app` was already a dependency (S-65's background/foreground detection), so no new native wiring was needed.

5. **Hand over.** Stubs go to `in-qa` (never `done`), the QA report names tests run, build result and what hardware cannot prove, and `work.mjs in-qa` moves the work item to QA. The worker then turns the banner green with the run's summary as its notes.

**Manual and analytics travel with every stub.** The analysis lists the English manual articles and the analytics the change affects; the rewrite updates the manual text and the telemetry spec; each sub-agent updates its stub's article and tracking code; each stub records them with `spec.mjs docs` before it can reach `in-qa`. Only `docs/manual/en/` is ever written by an agent: the nightly run translates it into the other languages with Ollama (`docs/spec/navigation-and-manual.md`).

**Manual and analytics travel with every stub.** The analysis lists the English manual articles and the analytics the change affects; the rewrite updates the manual text and the telemetry spec; each sub-agent updates its stub's article and tracking code; each stub records them, and the `docs/spec` files its finished behaviour was written into (`--spec`), with `spec.mjs docs` before it can reach `in-qa`. Only `docs/manual/en/` is ever written by an agent: the nightly run translates it into the other languages with Ollama (`docs/spec/navigation-and-manual.md`).

Rules that hold for both modes: never commit, push, deploy or touch AWS; the spec gate applies (the spec is authoritative, a line saying something was deliberately not built outranks a stub or an older note, and a conflict the answers do not settle becomes a blocking question, not code); a backend work item registers only `[Backend]` stubs in `SPEC_STUBS_BACKEND.md`.

- `SensorFacade.forSlot(1)` is the existing singleton. `forSlot(2)` lazily creates a second facade with its own backend, streams, battery, connection state and reconnect/backoff, so streams never cross and one ball dropping does not touch the other. Both share slot 1's `DiscoveryService`. `SensorFacade.hasSlot2()` tells whether it was ever created. E2E builds expose slot 2 as `window.__e2eSensorFacade2`.

- `selectBackend(deviceType, slot)`: mock and web work for both slots. On native, a Playwork ball gets its own `PlayworkBleBackend` for slot 2: that backend keeps all state per instance and sits on the multi-device `BleClient`, so **no second native plugin is needed**. A MetaWear ball (single Kotlin plugin) throws `SecondBallUnsupportedError`.

- `selectBackend(deviceType, slot)`: mock and web work for both slots. On native, a Playwork ball gets its own `PlayworkBleBackend` for slot 2: that backend keeps all state per instance and sits on the multi-device `BleClient`, so **no second native plugin is needed**. A MetaWear ball (every real ball today) gets `CapacitorBackend(2)`: Android's `SensorPlugin.kt` holds one `Link` per slot inside the one plugin (every call carries `slot`, every per-ball event is tagged with it, and the JS backend filters on it); iOS registers a second plugin instance, `SensorPlugin2` ("PlayworkSensor2"), with its own central manager and link. Slot 2 never scans: it is picked from slot 1's scan list and, on iOS, reconnects through the persisted MAC to peripheral map slot 1 wrote. `SecondBallUnsupportedError` stays defined but nothing throws it now. **Android compiles and installs; the two-link behaviour and all of iOS are unverified on hardware.**

questions.text: Section 19 requires a human-reviewed visual mockup (background art + both stability states) to be approved before any asset production or implementation begins, and explicitly forbids building the full game before that approval. The normal autonomous build flow (this skill's 'develop' mode) goes straight from a confirmed spec to planning tickets and building, with no mid-run visual-approval checkpoint. Should the Space Chase ticket plan include a dedicated 'mockup for review' stub that blocks every other stub until a person approves it, or should development proceed straight through using the written mechanics (which are already detailed) without that gate?
questions.answer: I want to clarify the visual design workflow. Rather than approving one overall mockup before development, I want you to generate the actual game assets according to the specification. For each asset, create several design variations and present them to us for selection. We will choose our preferred versions. Once the assets are approved, proceed with integrating them and implementing the game. Please adjust the ticket plan accordingly.

questions.text: Sections 1-18 call the two sensor inputs 'Force' and 'Accelerometer' and introduce 'Target Force'/'Force Threshold' as if new, but the app already has a squeezeThreshold field plus a shared pressure-bar 'Target Force' marker/label (S-176/S-197) that does exactly 'minimum threshold, reward at-or-above.' Should Space Chase's Force Threshold setting and Target Force simply be the existing squeezeThreshold + Target Force marker (now continuously driving horizontal speed instead of a pass/fail check), or does it need a genuinely separate kg-based mechanism? Default if unanswered: reuse squeezeThreshold and the existing Target Force marker/kg formula (deltaKpaToKg) — a parallel mechanism would fragment the Settings Tab.
questions.answer: Reuse the existing `squeezeThreshold` setting and the shared Target Force marker, including the existing `deltaKpaToKg` conversion logic. Do not introduce a separate kg-based mechanism or duplicate settings. The difference in Space Chase is gameplay behavior: Force should continuously control the spaceship's horizontal speed, while the existing Target Force remains the minimum threshold for achieving the required force performance. Keep the implementation consistent with the existing PLAYWORK Settings Tab and pressure-bar conventions.

questions.text: Section 13.5 limits the per-session Results Screen fields but says nothing about the Trainer Progress Report (cross-session trends). Wobble Island's 'Balance' section is the only existing per-game Progress Report addition. Should Space Chase get an equivalent Progress Report section (e.g. best-of-day Stabilized Isometric Performance)? Default if unanswered: no new Progress Report section for now.
questions.answer: Please add a **Stabilized Isometric Performance** chart to the Trainer Progress Report. - **Section title:** Physical Games Performance. - **Placement:** At the very bottom of the report, after all Cognitive Games Performance charts. - **X-axis:** Actual session date. - **Y-axis:** Stabilized Isometric Performance (%), ranging from 0% to 100%. - **Data:** Show the patient's performance trend across sessions over time. Since Space Chase replaces Wobble Island, remove the old Wobble Island (Balance) section from the Progress Report.

questions.text: Section 1 lists 'static squat exercises using a large PLAYBALL' alongside hand-grip/wall-press. Every other game (Wobble Island included) uses the standard region→extremity→laterality funnel with the physiotherapist defining the actual exercise position outside the app. Should Space Chase do the same, or does a squat-type exercise need its own funnel option? Default if unanswered: same as Wobble Island — standard funnel only, no new exercise-position setting.
questions.answer: Use the existing standard exercise selection funnel without any changes or additional exercise settings. The exercise types mentioned in the specification (hand grip, wall press, static squat, etc.) are examples of possible clinical uses only. The physiotherapist determines the actual exercise and patient position outside the app. These exercise types must not appear as options, settings, or part of the game's configuration or exercise selection process.
